newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt may issue up to 3 bln pound bonds- minister.
newsitem.headline: Egypt may issue up to 3 bln pound bonds- minister.

text.p: The Egyptian government may issue short-term Egyptian pound bonds worth up to three billion pounds ($880 million) on international markets to retire some of its local debt, Finance Minister Mohieddin el-Gharib said on Monday.

Gharib told Reuters the issue was likely to be in May and the bonds would probably have a 9.25 percent coupon. Four international financial institutions had already shown interest in marketing the bonds, he added.
"The bond issue is aimed at retiring local debt. It also will help put investor confidence in the pound," Gharib said.

Officials estimate Egypt's internal debt will reach 135 billion pounds in June 1997, up from 131 billion in June 1996. But the 1997 figure represents 54 percent of GDP, compared with 61 percent in the previous year.
The pound has been stable against the dollar for several years and exchange rates have even tended higher on the back of very large foreign inflows into Egypt's capital markets.

Global financial institutions have called on Egypt to develop its debt market and last month a consultant at the prime minister's office told Reuters the government wanted to put the pound on the international market by issuing two-year pound bonds on the Eurobond or foreign bond market.
He said it had approached international banks with a proposal to issue bonds for one billion pounds.
It was not clear if he was speaking about the same scheme as the one Gharib mentioned on Monday.

Either bond issue would be the first of its kind for Egypt but analysts say it would be cheaper for the government to have dollar-denominated bond issues, which would have lower interest rates than those on the pound.

The treasury issued local seven-year bonds worth four billion pounds in October 1996 with an 11 percent yield and five-year bonds worth three billion in May 1995 with a 12 percent yield. Both issues were oversubscribed.
But interest rates have declined steadily since the first issue. The average yield on treasury bills has fallen to just under 10 percent from about 10.8 percent in May 1995.
The government is preparing for an issue of long-term pound bonds to trade locally and replace some short-term t-bills. It has not when or how large the issue would be.
